Plotting

2026-10-21

Source: vignettes/plotting.Rmd
plotting.Rmd

This article shows the plotting functions in mcp: plot() for fitted values and predictions, plot_dpar() for distributional parameters, plot_pars() for parameters, and pp_check() for posterior predictive checks. All of them return ggplot2 objects, so they can be extended with regular ggplot2 code. The last section shows how to make your own plots from the same building blocks that plot() uses.

We use the bundled demo_fit, which is a three-segment model of the “demo” dataset:

library(mcp)
library(ggplot2)
demo_fit$model
## List of 3
##  $ response ~ 1
##  $ ~0 + time
##  $ ~1 + time

The default plot 

plot(demo_fit)

This shows:

  • The black dots are the data.
  • The gray lines are 25 joint posterior draws of the fitted values (expected response).
  • The blue curves on the x-axis are the posterior densities of the change points, one per chain.

Tweaking the plot

Showcasing some common arguments:

set.seed(42)  # Make lines replicable
plot(
  demo_fit,
  lines = 50,  # more fitted lines. Hide using `lines = 0`
  interval = c(
    "fitted",  # Show posterior fitted (red) interval
    "predict"  # Show posterior predictive (green) intervals
  ),
  width = 0.8, # Interval width
  cp_dens = FALSE  # Hide change point densities
)

Here, the intervals are computed using ndraws = 500 draws by default. Set ndraws = NULL to use all draws, which reduces Monte Carlo error at the cost of speed. For other quantiles, see making your own plots below.

Use geom_data = "line" for time series or geom_data = FALSE to hide the data.

Since the plots are ggplot2 objects, you can add themes, labels, etc.:

plot(demo_fit) +
  theme_bw(13) +
  labs(title = "Three segments", x = "Time (s)", y = "Response (ms)")

Prior predictive

Use prior = TRUE to see the prior predictive instead. This is a quick way to check what your priors imply when “put through” the model:

plot(demo_fit, prior = TRUE, lines = 100)

Categorical predictors, groups, and other predictors

In models with a categorical predictor, plot() draws a curve for each level and colors them automatically. Here, we use the “multiple” example, which has a categorical predictor (state) and a continuous predictor (z) in addition to the change-point variable (x):

fit = mcp_example("multiple", plot = FALSE)
fit$model
## List of 3
##  $ y ~ 1 + x:state + z
##  $ ~1 + x + state
##  $ ~0 + I(x^2) + same(state)
plot(fit)

Use color_by and facet_by to choose which categorical predictors or grouping columns to map to color and facets. For example, plot(fit, facet_by = "state") shows each state in a separate panel. With several categorical predictors, all of them must be identified by either color or facets, unless you set color_by = NULL.

Additional continuous predictors (z here) are held at their observed mean, as stated in the plot caption. Use at to evaluate at other values:

plot(fit, facet_by = "state", at = list(z = 0), interval = "fitted")

Note that the data points are not adjusted, so they are shown at their observed z.

For group-level effects, use facet_by to show the group-specific curves, e.g., plot(fit, facet_by = "id") for a model with (1 | id). Without it, the population-level curve is shown.

Scales

Use scale = "linear" to plot on the scale of the linear predictor, e.g., the log-odds for binomial() models. For binomial() and bernoulli() models, plot() shows success proportions by default; set rate = FALSE to show counts (see the binomial article).

Distributional parameters

plot_dpar() plots a distributional parameter, such as sigma, along the change-point variable. It takes most of the same arguments as plot(), but only interval = "fitted". Here, we use the “sigma” example, where the residual standard deviation changes at both change points:

fit_sigma = mcp_example("sigma", plot = FALSE)
fit_sigma$model
## List of 3
##  $ y ~ 1
##  $ ~0 + sigma(1 + x)
##  $ ~0 + x
plot_dpar(fit_sigma, dpar = "sigma", interval = "fitted")

The posterior predictive interval in plot() shows the same change in sigma on the scale of the data:

plot(fit_sigma, interval = "predict")

Other distributional parameters, e.g., "ar1" or "shape", are plotted the same way. Read more about modeling distributional parameters.

Parameters

plot_pars() plots the posterior (or prior with prior = TRUE) of parameters using bayesplot. The default is a “combo” of densities and trace plots, which is useful for checking convergence:

plot_pars(demo_fit, pars = c("cp_1", "cp_2"))

Use type to choose other bayesplot::mcmc_* plots, e.g., type = "dens_overlay", type = "trace", or type = "hex" (for the joint distribution of two parameters). pars = "population" (default) selects all population-level parameters and pars = "group" selects all group-level deviations; regex_pars selects parameters by name.

Posterior predictive checks

pp_check() compares the data to responses simulated from the posterior using bayesplot::ppc_*:

pp_check(demo_fit)

Use type for other checks, e.g., pp_check(fit, type = "ecdf_overlay"). Use facet_by to make a panel for each level of a categorical predictor or grouping column, e.g., for each state in the “multiple” example from above:

pp_check(fit, facet_by = "state")

Making your own plots

plot() evaluates fitted() and predict() on an x-grid made by interpolate_newdata(). This grid has extra resolution around the change points, all combinations of categorical predictor levels, and additional continuous predictors held at their observed means (or at at). You can use the same building blocks to make any plot you want:

newdata = interpolate_newdata(demo_fit)
head(newdata)
## # A tibble: 6 × 1
##    time
##   <dbl>
## 1 0.619
## 2 1.62 
## 3 2.62 
## 4 3.62 
## 5 4.62 
## 6 5.62

For example, below is a ribbon of the 95% central interval of the fitted values. In addition, a quantile (median) is added using summary = FALSE and a “manual” summary.

# Fitted and intervals
fitted_summary = fitted(demo_fit, newdata = newdata)

# A custom quantile (here median)
fitted_median = fitted(demo_fit, newdata = newdata, summary = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::summarise(.epred = median(.epred), .by = time)

# Plot!
ggplot(fitted_summary, aes(x = time, y = .mean)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower, ymax = .upper), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .epred), data = fitted_median, color = "red") +
  geom_point(aes(y = response), data = demo_fit$data)

You can add the same layer to plot(), e.g., plot(demo_fit) + geom_line(aes(x = time, y = .epred), data = fitted_median, inherit.aes = FALSE). inherit.aes = FALSE is needed because plot() maps internal columns that are not in fitted_median.

The draws follow tidybayes conventions (.draw, .epred, .prediction), so you can also use tidybayes and ggdist to summarise and plot them, e.g., multiple interval widths:

library(tidybayes)
predict(demo_fit, newdata = newdata, summary = FALSE) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = .prediction)) +
  stat_lineribbon(.width = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.95), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y = response), data = demo_fit$data) +
  scale_fill_brewer()

See also the fits and predictions article for out-of-sample predictions and forecasting with future change points, and the missing responses article for adding imputations to plot().
